Commonplace Books: A History of Reading and Remembering

Long before search engines and note-taking apps, readers kept commonplace books: bound volumes into which they copied passages, observations, and fragments worth remembering. A commonplace book was not a diary but a working archive, organised by theme rather than by date, meant to be reread and rearranged over years.

The margins of these books were often as important as the passages themselves. Readers filled the empty space around a quoted line with their own marginalia, arguing with the author, drawing connections to other texts, or simply marking a passage that struck them. Historians now treat this marginalia as evidence of how ideas actually moved between books and minds.

John Locke, among others, published a method for indexing a commonplace book so that any passage could be found again quickly. His system used a grid of letters and vowels to file entries under headings, turning a personal scrapbook into something closer to a searchable database, centuries before the word existed.

What makes the commonplace book tradition useful today is not the paper and ink but the discipline behind it: capture widely, annotate honestly, and revisit often. A digital tool that only stores links without inviting annotation misses half of what made the practice valuable in the first place.
